So, it's been over two weeks since I said I'd post this, and I believe I've had enough fun with this in TF2 to take the time and make this post, now.

 

There are lots of things you can do for projectile prediction in games, but this post is going to be focusing on three things: position extrapolation based on target velocity and projectile's predicted time to hit, gravity, and further precision ideas.

 

time = distance / projectileacceleration

Figure you're trying to find the time it'd take to travel 100 miles going 50 miles per hour, the time to get there would be 2 hours. Once you have your time, it's a matter of extrapolation of the current position: predictedpos = pos + targetvelocity * time

 

What if your target is in the air or your projectile doesn't fly without gravitational pull? You have your predicted position from above, but let's assume the target is in the air and is being effected by gravity.

gravitydelta = 0.5 * gravity * time ^ 2

 

So for target gravity, you'd need to do this: predictedpos.z -= 0.5 * targetgravity * time ^ 2 and for projectile gravity, you can just pretend the gravity is added onto the predicted position, as well. predictedpos.z += 0.5 * projectilegravity * time ^ 2

 

This is all fine and dandy, but you're most likely aiming at a moving target, right? How far have they moved since the projectile had been fired? Depending on how fast movement in the game is or how slow your projectile may be, you most likely will also want targetvelocity prediction. This is done by reiterating these calculations a couple times for more refined times.

 

After you extrapolate (don't forget to add gravity and all that fun stuff) with your new time, your basic projectile prediction should look a bit like this: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B-VclWqxpBs

 

(Note: Some projectiles may have other attributes you might have to account for. Air resistance comes to mind, but there may be other things to account for.)

 

What if you predict your enemy to fly through a wall/floor/ceiling? Here's where it starts getting a bit tougher to make it more precise. The next major step is to simulate movement. This can be done through ingame functions for movement prediction or by true ghetto simulation. TF2 is one hell of a dynamic game, so you can't really just write your own movement simulation and think it'll be alright. This is your call, on whichever game you hope to apply this to, but I'd recommend looking into the game engine's movement simulation functions.

 

Alright, you stopped your aim logic from predicting targets flying through walls, but what if they start walking the opposite way they were headed halfway through your projectile's predicted trajectory? This would be the most fun part where you look into creating movement prediction/movement bias prediction towards different situations/states the target faces in the game. You're gonna be on your own on this one, but I'm sure with the right setup, you can reliably predict how they will react.

 

Oh, and don't mess up tracing. Any time somebody traces from their shootposition to the target origin is too many times. Trace to the predicted position, if you do any tracing at all. Also, you should trace the projectile like the game does. Use bounding box traces when necessary, and try to atleast intermittently (if not exactly as the server would) trace the projectile's arc, if it's effected by gravity.

 

I've had plenty of fun with this the last few weeks, and I hope you guys do, as well. tl;dr https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B-VclWqxpBs
